newsitem.title: GERMANY: German court rejects IG Farben claim on land.
newsitem.headline: German court rejects IG Farben claim on land.

text.p: Germany's highest court on Thursday rejected a complaint by chemical group IG Farben, finally ending the group's long-running attempts to get back property confiscated after World War Two.
IG Farben, the maker of the Zyklon gas the Nazis used to kill Jews, had appealed to Germany's constitutional court that a ruling, handed down in May, was unconstitutional.

But the court refused to hear the complaint, saying IG Farben's complaint lacked any chance of success. It referred to previous rulings that property in east Germany which was seized under Soviet military occupation in 1945-49 should not be returned to its former owners.
IG Farben in west Germany was split up after the war into BASF AG, Bayer AG and Hoechst AG, but a shell company, IG Farben in Liquidation, still exists to group outstanding asset claims.
It demanded the return of 17 plants in the east German state of Saxony Anhalt.
IG Farben was not immediately available for comment, but participation certificates in the group fell 6.9 percent in bourse trading after the news was announced.

At issue were about 3.3 million hectares (8.2 million acres) or a third of east German agricultural land, mostly the hereditary estates of the Prussian nobility which were broken up and given to peasants or converted into collective farms.

The German government always insisted that the finality of the confiscations was a key Soviet demand during negotiations to end the rights of the Allied post-war occupiers and return full sovereignty to Germany upon unification in 1990.

But three years later former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev denied that he had insisted a united Germany must respect the land seizures, sparking the latest wave of claims from a variety of people.
